newsitem.title: USA: U.S. puzzles aftermath of China Hong Kong takeover.
newsitem.headline: U.S. puzzles aftermath of China Hong Kong takeover.

text.p: For President Bill Clinton's foreign policy advisers, China's takeover of Hong Kong in July is a three-dimensional puzzle they are doing in the dark.

With just three months to go before the guard changes on July 1, fathoming Beijing's true intentions for the former British colony preoccupies a legion of China experts in the U.S. government and elsewhere.

Congress has served notice it wants the Clinton administration to press Beijing to live up to its vow to create "one country, two systems" and not backslide on promises to maintain democratic freedoms.

U.S. China experts say Beijing has largely laid its plans for Hong Kong. In the near term, they say, the chief potential problem is how far China will go to suppress dissent. If it feels its security is threatened, a harsh crackdown in the prosperous enclave of 6.4 million people could invite a U.S. rebuke.

But the experts feel it is unlikely that isolated targeting of individual Hong Kong dissenters would cause more than a ripple in U.S. relations, which have already weathered storms over human rights, Taiwan and weapons proliferation.

"We have already seen what China's intentions are towards Hong Kong and they aren't very favourable," Columbia University China specialist Andrew Nathan said. "On the predictable issues (such as civil rights, trade and other legal problems) we already know, and it's not good. It's how they react to demonstrations if they should develop," he said.

"I think you'll see a crackdown," Nathan said. "They have certainly set things up for that to happen" by vowing to scrap a democratically elected legislature and take away certain civil liberties, he added.

Vice President Al Gore is to discuss the future of Hong Kong when he visits Beijing this month, the most senior U.S. official to visit China since army troops crushed pro-democracy protests around Tiananmen Square in 1989. Gore was to pave the way for an exchange of presidential visits but criticism of alleged White House influence peddling involving Chinese interests has become an obstacle.

Gore follows Secretary of State Madeleine Albright who stopped in Beijing last month when an invitation to witness the handover in Hong Kong was discussed. U.S. officials said privately that Albright has not ruled it out.
House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich is leading a congressional delegation to Hong Kong and China on March 23.

Congress put added pressure on the administration when the House voted 416-1 this month for a bill that calls on Beijing to honour a treaty with Britain promising extensive autonomy for Hong Kong after the handover. China's Foreign Ministry called this a "gross interference in China's internal affairs."

The House asked Beijing to reconsider its repeal of Hong Kong's bill of rights and to keep independent the civil service, judiciary, police and anti-corruption agency. The Senate is expected to follow the House lead.
"Hong Kong's autonomy is clearly under attack," said Ben Gilman, a New York Republican who chairs the House International Relations Commitee, in explaining why the measure was needed.

The bill also focuses on getting the Clinton administration to ensure that China does not use Hong Kong as a funnel for goods shipped to the United States in violation of trade agreements. The United States will continue to treat its $24 billion in annual trade with Hong Kong separately.
But trade and political differences are not the top concern for Emily Yow, a Hong Kong resident who has been attending school in Washington for the past four years.

"I made plans months ago to go back for the handover to find out where I stand," she said, adding that thousands of the estimated 110,000 Hong Kong passport holders living in the United States are doing the same.

China has not made clear if overseas residents will have the right to return to live in Hong Kong if they are out of the country at the time of the handover. Airline spokesmen call the flood of bookings unprecedented. Flights for weeks on either side of the handover date have been sold out for months.
